description: Next-step Spanish for A2–B1 learners: plural you, go and come, should, negative words, reasons, purpose, just-did and knowing. Latin American Spanish (broadly neutral).

terms.definition: Means 'you' for two or more people, friends and strangers alike, all over Latin America.
terms.example: ¿Ustedes quieren algo de tomar? — Do you guys want something to drink?
terms.discussion: It takes the same verb form as ellos: ustedes tienen, ustedes van. Vosotros is Spain only, so you can skip it.

terms.definition: Says you move from here to another place: voy al trabajo, ¿vas al centro?
terms.example: Voy al súper, ¿necesitas algo? — I'm going to the store, need anything?
terms.discussion: A plus el always becomes al: voy al banco, never 'voy a el banco'. With la nothing changes: voy a la playa.

terms.definition: Gives the purpose of an action, like English 'to' or 'in order to'.
terms.example: Llamo para pedir una pizza. — I'm calling to order a pizza.
terms.anti_example: Not 'llamo pedir' or 'llamo por pedir': when 'to' means purpose, Spanish needs para.

terms.definition: Covers 'nobody' and 'not anybody': not one single person.
terms.example: Nadie contesta el teléfono en la oficina. — Nobody's answering the phone at the office.
terms.anti_example: Not 'no hay alguien en casa' for 'there isn't anybody home': say 'no hay nadie en casa'.

terms.definition: Gives advice about the right thing to do, like English 'should'.
terms.example: Debes ir al médico hoy. — You should see a doctor today.
terms.discussion: It sounds like friendly advice. For rules and real must-dos, people usually say tener que instead.

terms.definition: Answers the question 'why?' by putting the reason right after it, like 'because'.
terms.example: Llego tarde porque hay mucho tráfico. — I'm late because there's a lot of traffic.
terms.anti_example: Not 'porque' in the question: ask '¿por qué?', two words with an accent, and answer 'porque…'.

terms.definition: Covers knowing a fact, like a name or a time, and knowing how to do something.
terms.example: ¿Sabes cómo se llama el mesero? — Do you know the waiter's name?
terms.anti_example: Not 'sé a María' for 'I know María': for people and places, say 'conozco a María'.

terms.definition: Says something happened a moment ago: acabo de llegar means 'I just got here'.
terms.example: No, gracias, acabo de comer. — No thanks, I just ate.
terms.anti_example: Not 'solo comí' for 'I just ate': that means 'I only ate'. Say 'acabo de comer'.

terms.definition: Means 'never' or 'not ever': something doesn't happen at any time.
terms.example: Mi papá nunca toma café en la noche. — My dad never drinks coffee at night.
terms.discussion: Two word orders work: nunca before the verb, or no before the verb and nunca at the end: no toma café nunca.

terms.definition: Describes moving toward the place where the speaker is: come here, come to my place.
terms.example: ¿Vienes a mi fiesta el sábado? — Are you coming to my party on Saturday?
terms.anti_example: Not 'ya vengo' when your mom calls you: say '¡Ya voy!'. You go toward her, so it's ir.

terms.definition: Means 'not a single one' or 'none', about things or people you can count.
terms.example: No tengo ninguna pregunta, gracias. — I don't have any questions, thanks.
terms.discussion: Before a masculine noun it becomes ningún: ningún problema. It stays singular where English says 'any questions'.

terms.definition: Talks about knowing a person or a place firsthand: a friend, a city, a café.
terms.example: ¿Conoces Cartagena? Es muy bonita. — Have you been to Cartagena? It's really pretty.
terms.discussion: With a person, add a: conozco a tu hermano. In the past it often means 'met': la conocí en Lima.

relationships.description: Both mean 'know': saber for facts and skills, conocer for people and places.
Venir is toward where the speaker is; ir is toward anywhere else, even when English says 'coming'.
Porque gives a reason with a full sentence; para plus a verb gives the goal.
After the verb, both need no in front of the verb: no viene nadie, no viene nunca.
